public_notes.title: Reserved Hunting Rights
public_notes.text: The Tribe's Natural Resources page connects its members' hunting rights to an Act of April 29, 1874 and a September 21, 1978 Brunot consent decree. It places those agreements within its account of wildlife management. This is the Tribe's description of reserved rights, not a current legal determination, hunting regulation or permission for visitors to enter or hunt.

public_notes.title: Water, Health And Future Generations
public_notes.text: On its undated Environmental Program page, the Tribe describes work with Ute Mountain Ute communities to conserve resources and protect public health for future generations. Listed areas include water conservation, environmental education, and water and air quality. These are the Tribe's published program descriptions, not independent measurements of environmental conditions or proof that a service operates on a particular date.

public_notes.title: Learning Across Generations
public_notes.text: The Tribe's Cultural/Language Program page describes strengthening cultural identity and teaching youth about Ute Mountain Ute ancestry. It also reports that Ute Mountain Ute and Southern Ute worked together on a fourth-grade Ute curriculum. The page gives no project date or completion details. This is a reported collaboration between distinct Tribes, not evidence that their governments or educational programs are interchangeable.

public_notes.title: Promises, Pressure And Scattered Allotments
public_notes.text: The Tribe's history explains that Apache prisoners were told Fort Sill would be their permanent home, then pressured to leave as a condition of freedom. It describes a Mescalero invitation, urged by government agents, to relocate and families who continued to demand promised land at Fort Sill. A later compromise placed those who remained on scattered allotments near Apache and Fletcher. These were different paths under coercion, not interchangeable present-day governments.

public_notes.title: Rebuilding Government And A Land Base
public_notes.text: The Tribe's history records a land-claim settlement in the mid-1970s and the approval of a constitution. It then describes acquiring land in Oklahoma and in its New Mexico and Arizona homelands. Its government page explains how the General Council and Business Committee share governing responsibilities. These sources describe rebuilding institutions and a land base after displacement; they do not establish present property boundaries or legal jurisdiction.

public_notes.title: Language And Living Continuity
public_notes.text: The Tribe's public Cultural and Language Program page describes preserving Tribal history and teaching the Chiricahua language. It describes collecting historical resources and developing learning materials for Tribal members. These are the Tribe's stated program purposes. An undated program description does not verify today's classes or their outcomes. These preservation goals belong alongside the history of imprisonment and displacement.

public_notes.title: Land Pressure And Dispossession
public_notes.text: The Nation describes the Treaty at Nations Ford as an exchange in which it relinquished land in return for promises of another tract and payment. Its account places the agreement amid settler pressure and the threat of removal west. This is an attributed history of dispossession, not a current finding about land title or jurisdiction.

public_notes.title: Constitution And Collective Action
public_notes.text: The Nation's account dates the creation of a constitution to 1944. It records a petition to Congress for federal recognition in 1973 and an updated constitution adopted in 1975. Its history links these steps to the community's effort to regain recognition. These milestones add context to the later settlement; they do not decide a present recognition dispute.

public_notes.title: Stewardship And Community Planning
public_notes.text: The Nation describes its Realty program as protecting and managing trust- and fee-owned lands. Its transportation program also describes public meetings to gather input on planned projects. These are the Nation's descriptions of its work, not independent measurements of results, a current land-title ruling or a guarantee that a listed project is complete.

official_resources.purpose: The Tribe describes language and youth education, including reported fourth-grade curriculum work with Southern Ute. Project dates, current schedules and completion are not established.

official_resources.label: Fort Sill Apache government explained by the Tribe
official_resources.purpose: The Tribe describes the General Council and Business Committee and their roles in governing. This resource is not an independent audit or an endorsement of outcomes, current officeholders or election dates.

official_resources.label: Fort Sill Apache cultural and language preservation
official_resources.purpose: The Tribe describes its public history-preservation and Chiricahua language-teaching goals. This listing does not reproduce ceremonial or restricted knowledge and does not verify a current class timetable or program outcomes.

official_resources.label: Catawba Nation history and constitutional organizing
official_resources.purpose: The Nation's account of land pressure, the Nations Ford agreement and constitutional organizing in 1944, 1973 and 1975. Its sections give conflicting 1951 and 1959 federal-status years; neither year is adopted here.

official_resources.label: Catawba land stewardship and community planning
official_resources.purpose: Read the Nation's descriptions of Realty and transportation planning, including public input. An undated program description is not independent proof of current project completion or legal title.

official_resources.label: Black Snake Farm and dated market information
official_resources.purpose: Own farm description and market FAQ labeled July 15, 2025. It states grant funding through June 2026. Current funding, schedule and eligibility are not confirmed by this source review.
